column1: # 2장 말투 지시. 열: 조각 앞머리 → 지시(영어, 짧게). 서술 지시는 장면이 끝날 때까지 이어진다.
# 대사는 스페인어 앞머리로 찾는다. @scene 행은 장면 설명(장면 끝까지 모든 요청에 붙는다). 11-10부터 지시가 바뀌어도 요청을 나누지 않는다.

column2: Early morning in Montse's kitchen. Valentina, a young Argentine lodger, comes in in her pajamas and introduces herself with the Argentine "vos". Montse, from Barcelona, corrects "vos" to Spain's "tú", half teasing; Valentina laughs it off. Yuna is new and only knows a little Spanish.
bright, surprised to see a new face
correcting Valentina like a teacher, dry, with a click of the tongue; stress "tú"
chatty and cheerful; she says "¿Y vos?" again without noticing
tapping her chest, shortening her name
puzzled: to her "vale" is the word for "okay"
curious, a little out of breath

column1: # 11-10 추가: 나머지 장면(새벽, 아침 식탁, cashe, 광장, 열쇠공방)

column2: Yuna wakes at five in the morning in Barcelona, jet-lagged, listening to unfamiliar street sounds. She remembers Montse's last word the night before, "mañana" (tomorrow), and takes out her grandmother's key. Quiet and expectant.

Breakfast in Montse's kitchen. Montse calls Yuna "nena" and asks "¿qué tal?"; Yuna surprises her by answering in Catalan, "Bon dia". Montse names the food word by word (pan con tomate, con, café con leche), then points at things like a teacher to show "el" for masculine and "la" for feminine words. Warm and light.
trying the Catalan greeting she learned yesterday, a little proud
naming the dish slowly, pointing at the bread, then the tomato

column1: Sí. Café con leche, por favor.
column2: a whole sentence, careful and pleased
pointing at each thing like a teacher; stress "el"

Montse gets ready to take Yuna to the street on her grandmother's envelope. Vale, from Buenos Aires, says "calle" the Rioplatense way, "cashe"; Montse corrects her, separating the syllables "Ca-lle" with the Spanish "ll", as she has for eight months, and Vale says it is the same thing. Brisk, with friendly bickering.
asking where, a word she learned from the taxi driver

column1: A la calle de tu abuela.

column2: cutting in, curious; Rioplatense "sh" sound in "cashe"
correcting her pronunciation, separating the syllables; stress the "ll"

Montse walks Yuna through Gràcia to the Plaça de la Vila. She teaches the Catalan and Castilian names (plaça / plaza, rellotge / reloj) and corrects "esto" to "eso" for something farther away. Yuna realizes "Rellotger" means clockmaker, and Montse shows her the corner where the clockmaker's street used to be: now a phone shop. Curious at first, then quietly sad.
pointing at the sign, teaching both names; stress "Plaça" and "plaza"

column1: Rellotger… el señor de los relojes.
column2: slowly, explaining what the word means
not fine, but saying so, quietly

Montse leads Yuna down a dark alley to an old locksmith's shop and explains its name in Catalan and Castilian (serralleria / cerrajería: a shop of "llaves", keys). It is closed for the August holidays. In the window Yuna finds a key identical to her grandmother's, and Montse, looking up at a closed window above the shop, quietly says a name: Marc. Disappointment turning to hushed discovery.
reading the sign, teaching the two names
linking the word to the keys; stress "llaves"
reading the notice, mildly disappointed, explaining
very quietly, a name said almost to herself
